_comment: Mutations for the three `?format=csv` exports, scored against csv_run.sh — the harness that serves the Python from a worktree of 2baabe6~1. This spec exists because that harness was written AFTER the reference was deleted, which makes it the one case list in this directory whose author could not be corrected by a failing run while writing it. Everything here is a bug a CSV port plausibly has: LF instead of CRLF, quoting too much or too little, defanging a number, dropping the header, exporting another org. Several change bytes that a CSV parser does not care about at all — which is the point: the harness compares bytes, and a compliance archive is bytes. `restart_rust` is false because csv_run.sh builds and restarts its own tier pair on 8010/8011; mutate.py's tiers.sh path would refuse, the Python it wants being gone.

mutations.name: LF line endings instead of CRLF
mutations._why: RFC 4180 says CRLF and `csv.writer(lineterminator="\r\n")` writes it. Every spreadsheet opens the LF file identically, so nothing downstream complains — and the archived bytes differ from every export that came before.

mutations.name: every field quoted
mutations._why: QUOTE_ALL parses the same as QUOTE_MINIMAL and is a different file. The tempting mutation: quoting everything is *safer* in isolation and wrong as a port.

mutations.name: a newline inside a field is not quoted
mutations._why: The one omission that corrupts the file rather than just differing: an unquoted LF ends the record, so a details column containing a newline silently becomes two rows and every column after it shifts.

mutations.name: an embedded quote is not doubled
mutations._why: `""` is how RFC 4180 escapes a quote inside a quoted field. Without the doubling the field terminates early and the rest of the row is unparseable.

mutations.name: formula leaders are not defanged
mutations._why: The OWASP mitigation. MCP key names and node names inside audit details are caller-controlled, so `=HYPERLINK(...)` in an export executes when an admin opens it.

mutations.name: a hyphen is not treated as a formula leader
mutations._why: `-` is on Python's list, and dropping just that one is the plausible mistake: it looks like a minus sign rather than an attack. The fixture has a username of `-5`.

mutations.name: integers are defanged like strings
mutations._why: The reason Cell::Raw exists. `duration_ms = -5` is an int in the Python row builder and is NOT defanged; treating every cell as text turns it into `'-5`, which a spreadsheet then sorts as text.

mutations.name: the header row is defanged too
mutations._why: `writer.writerow(header)` passes plain strings through the escape path without defanging. No current column name starts with a leader, so this is invisible today — and it is one renamed column from being visible.
mutations.equivalent: No column name in the three exports starts with =, +, -, @, tab or CR, so Text and Raw render identically for every header this code can produce. Recorded rather than deleted: it is the mutation that would catch a future column named `-duration`.

mutations.name: the export has no header row
mutations._why: An export whose first row is data looks fine in a spreadsheet — the first audit entry simply becomes the column names — and every downstream parser silently loses a row.

mutations.name: a NULL text column exports as the word null
mutations._why: `log.ip_address or ""` — a NULL is an empty field, not a literal. The fixture has NULLs in every nullable column of all three tables.

mutations.name: a NULL duration exports as zero
mutations._why: `duration_ms if ... is not None else ""`. Zero is a measurement; empty is the absence of one, and a tool that never reported a duration is not a tool that took no time.

mutations.name: the filename loses its date
mutations._why: The date is what makes a month of exports sort chronologically in a download folder, and Content-Disposition is compared by the harness because it is what the browser saves the file as.

mutations.name: the org id is not sanitised into the filename
mutations._why: The org id is Clerk's string. A quote in it breaks the quoted Content-Disposition value; a control character makes HeaderValue::from_str fail and the export 500s.
mutations.equivalent: The fixture's org id is `self-host`, which safe_segment leaves untouched — so this harness cannot tell the two apart, and the first version of this mutation did not even compile (a missing comma), which scored as `no result` rather than as the MISS it is. What catches it is the unit test `filenames_are_dated_and_sanitised`, which feeds it `a"b/../c\n`. Kept as the record of which check owns this, because a fixture whose org id contained a quote would move it here and that is worth knowing.

mutations.name: the download is cacheable
mutations._why: An audit export is one org's compliance data. A proxy or a shared browser cache holding it is a real privacy regression, and `Cache-Control: no-store` is the only thing preventing it.

mutations.name: the content type loses its charset
mutations._why: `text/csv; charset=utf-8`. The fixture holds non-ASCII, and a client that believes a bare `text/csv` is Latin-1 renders mojibake.

mutations.name: the CSV window ignores the caller's filters
mutations._why: The export must cover the rows the auditor was looking at. Dropping the WHERE clause exports the whole org — and, with org_id in it, every org.
mutations.old: FROM audit_log{where_sql} ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50000"
mutations.new: FROM audit_log ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50000"

mutations.name: the export is ordered oldest first
mutations._why: `ORDER BY timestamp DESC` matches the JSON page beside it. Reversing it is a different file with the same rows, which no assertion about row COUNT could catch.
mutations.old: FROM mcp_activity_logs{where_sql} ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50000"
mutations.new: FROM mcp_activity_logs{where_sql} ORDER BY timestamp ASC LIMIT 50000"

mutations.name: the stream export column order follows the JSON body
mutations._why: The export leads with `accessed_at` so a spreadsheet sorted by column A is sorted by time; the JSON body leads with `id`. Two orders that are each defensible and only one of which is the Python's. Note what this mutation actually does: it reorders the HEADER only, since the cells come from the SQL in its own order — so it is caught as a header that no longer describes its data, which is a worse bug than the one the name describes.

mutations.name: CSV honours the JSON row limit
mutations._why: The CSV branch deliberately bypasses `limit`/`offset` for a flat 50,000-row window — an auditor wants a window, not a page. Honouring `?limit=1` would hand them one row and no error.
mutations.old: FROM audit_log{where_sql} ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50000"
mutations.new: FROM audit_log{where_sql} ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1"

mutations.name: the format parameter is validated after the branch
mutations._why: `q.finish()` runs before the CSV hand-off, so `?format=csv&limit=0` is a 422 and not a download. Dropping it lets an invalid request succeed — and it compiles, which I wrongly expected it not to: `limit` and `offset` are still read by the JSON path below. Caught by the four 422 cases in csv_diff.py.
